Further Reading

The Ledger asks a few plain questions of local decisions: Is it decided close to home? Does it help ordinary families own and keep a place? Who pays? These are the books and essays behind those questions, plus a few that disagree with us. None of it is required. Start with the first section.

Start here

Localism: Coming Home to Catholic Social Teaching, Dale Ahlquist and Michael Warren Davis. A recent, readable case for local ownership, local work, and local government.

Small Is Beautiful: Economics as if People Mattered, E. F. Schumacher (1973). On scale, and why bigger is not always better for the people it is supposed to serve.

Chattanooga Civics. A local project in Chattanooga, Tennessee that helps residents see what their city and county governments are doing and how to respond. It is a good model for learning how your own government works, and it is close to what the Ledger tries to do.

The tradition

The Outline of Sanity, G. K. Chesterton (1926). The classic case for widely held property and for small, local things.

What's Wrong with the World, G. K. Chesterton (1910). On the family, the home, and why ordinary people should own a stake in their place.

The Servile State, Hilaire Belloc (1912). How concentrated wealth and a large government can grow together, with ordinary people dependent on both.

An Essay on the Restoration of Property, Hilaire Belloc (1936). Belloc's proposals for spreading ownership more widely.

Distributism Basics: Foundational Principles, David W. Cooney (2020). A modern, plain-language introduction. His articles are free online at practicaldistributism.com.

Church teaching on property and subsidiarity

Rerum Novarum, Pope Leo XIII (1891). The foundation of modern Catholic social teaching, on work, property, and the family.

Quadragesimo Anno, Pope Pius XI (1931). The classic statement of subsidiarity: higher bodies should help lower ones, not take over their work.

Centesimus Annus, Pope John Paul II (1991). A look at markets, property, and the state after the fall of communism.

Laudato Si', Pope Francis (2015). On caring for the natural world. It is a useful reminder that this tradition takes the land and water seriously, which matters for items like wetlands and stream buffers.

Place, land, and local government

The Unsettling of America, Wendell Berry (1977). On land, farming, and what is lost when a place is managed from far away.

Governing the Commons, Elinor Ostrom (1990). How communities have managed shared resources like water and fisheries without waiting for a distant authority.

Strong Towns, Charles Marohn (2019). A practical look at how cities pay for themselves and how land-use rules affect ordinary households. It does not come from the distributist tradition, but it asks many of our questions about cost and who pays.

The Death and Life of Great American Cities, Jane Jacobs (1961). On why small businesses, short blocks, and old buildings matter to a neighborhood.

Where we might be wrong

"What's Wrong with Distributism," Thomas Woods (2002), on the Mises Institute website. A well-known critique of the whole approach.

"Credit Union Economics," Michael McCabe. A distributist reply to Woods, available at practicaldistributism.com. Read the two together.

If you know a book or essay that should be on this list, especially one that disagrees with us, write to thecorcoran@gmail.com.
